needs.text: ask why government does not eliminate online anonymity by mandating unique accounts linked to SSN or ID

social security numbers or unique identification
implementing mandatory identity verification for online activities poses multiple practical and policy challenges
creating and managing a database linking online accounts to unique IDs requires heavy tech infrastructure investment
forcing citizens to share sensitive personal information raises major privacy concerns
mandatory identity requirements risk disproportionately disadvantaging marginalized communities lacking resources or access
users can circumvent identity checks using proxy servers or virtual private networks
balancing privacy, security, and accessibility is necessary because online identity mandates carry severe trade-offs
argue that progress can still be made to reduce fraud, identity theft, and cyberbullying without total anonymity
online fraud, identity theft, and cyberbullying
alternative security measures can mitigate risks without requiring government-issued ID verification
require email address verification before account creation or posting
email verification prevents spammers and trolls from generating disposable anonymous accounts
enforce strong password policies and frequent password updates
complex passwords protect accounts from credential theft and unauthorized access
implement two-factor authentication requiring secondary confirmation codes
ask whether eliminating anonymity improves behavioral accountability and aids law enforcement against criminals
ending online anonymity would increase user accountability and facilitate criminal investigations
potential benefits to accountability and law enforcement must be weighed against severe privacy and equity drawbacks
technical bypasses, infrastructure costs, and civil liberties risks make direct government ID mandates problematic
targeted security practices provide effective risk mitigation while preserving essential privacy and accessibility
